root_quality_holds.reason: Latin litera/littera and stems liter/litter are attested; bare lit as a distinct letter stem is not independently established. Its occurrence at the beginning of a longer stem is insufficient.

In pronounce and announce the supported historical base is Latin nuntiare and French -nonc-; bare noun is not documented here as an independent declare-form. English noun and pronoun derive from Latin nomen name, a different sense and family.

Optimal/optimum are from Latin optimus best, whose historical decomposition has competing analyses; an independent opt stem meaning best is not established by these sources. Existing optim best is better supported.

Wordsmyth lists scen as a teaching lookup alongside scend, but historical dictionaries document scend/scens rather than an independently attested scen morpheme. Hold this truncated lookup under the independent word-formation policy; retain the separate Greek scen booth entry.

The sequence surr crosses the Latin assimilated prefix sub- and the following regere-derived stem; it is not established as an independent root. The complete documented historical stem surrect is retained.

Independent dictionaries attest Greek anthrop-/anthropo- for human, but a standalone anthr- meaning human was not established; anthr- in chemical terminology is a distinct form. Retain all 14 reviewed words under the already supported anthrop and anthro entries, and preserve the original target and examples as a reversible quality hold.

All 12 examples are descendants of Latin ambulare or shortened ambl-; none examined establishes amb alone as an independently functioning historical walk stem. Isolate as insufficiently supported, not disproven. Wordsmyth and GRE study guide explicitly list amb as a teaching root, so this is not an absence-of-all-sources claim: those lists do not demonstrate separate historical segmentation, and the same examples are explained by full ambul/ambl. A documented project policy might intentionally retain amb as a lookup-only clipped alias, but it must be labeled as such rather than as an independently substantiated stem.
Both example words trace to Latin vinum or French descendants, but competing accounts do not establish an independent Latin vint = wine root. English vint is a later back-formation.

Greek source combines lykos wolf with anthropos human, so lycan crosses the historical boundary; one teaching list uses lycan as a lookup but does not independently establish a modern wolf prefix. The two disputed exact relations and root classification are held pending, with original source and past acceptances preserved.
